etymology: Hebrew bela’, “devouring” or “destruction,” the name of the first king who reigned in Edom; not to be confounded with Bela the son of Benjamin, nor with the town Bela which is Zoar.
biblical_def: Bela the son of Beor was the FIRST king who reigned in the land of Edom, before ever a king reigned over the children of Israel (Gen 36:31–32). The name of his city was Dinhabah. He stands at the head of that early line of Edomite crowns set down in the register of Esau’s generations, and again in the chronicle of the kings (1Chr 1:43). The Holy Ghost is careful to mark that these kings of Esau rose up while Jacob’s seed had as yet no king at all, but were sojourners and bondmen and wilderness pilgrims. Herein is a deep providence: the profane brother’s house was crowned early, and Israel waited long; yet Edom’s crowns rose only to perish, while the sceptre promised to Judah should not depart till Shiloh come (Gen 49:10). Bela the son of Beor reigned, and Bela died (Gen 36:33); the very next clause is his grave. So it is written of all the kings of Edom in their order, each reigning and each dying, that the reader may learn how the pomp of the ungodly is but for a moment. Esau profanely sold his birthright (Heb 12:16); his sons gained earthly thrones and lost them. But the King of Israel liveth and reigneth for ever, and of His kingdom there shall be no end.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God over the thrones of men: He sets up kings and removeth kings (Dan 2:21), and He crowned Edom early only that Edom might fall. Esau was the profane brother who despised his birthright (Heb 12:16), and his sons reigned and died in their order. Let the reader weigh the perishing crowns of Edom against the King of Israel whose throne is for ever and ever.

etymology: Hebrew yobab, “a desert” or “howling,” the name of the second king of Edom, the son of Zerah of Bozrah, who reigned after Bela.
biblical_def: Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in Edom after the death of Bela (Gen 36:33). He is the second of the kings who reigned in the land of Esau before any king reigned over Israel (Gen 36:31). Bozrah, his city, was a chief stronghold of Edom, named afterward by the prophets as the place where the LORD would do His sore work of judgment upon the seed of Esau (Isa 34:6). The record of Jobab is brief and sober: he reigned, and he died, and another rose up in his stead (Gen 36:34). So runs the whole catalogue of Edom’s kings, a procession of crowns laid one by one in the dust. The genealogist of the Chronicles repeats the same names that the reader of the latter days might know how ancient and how short-lived were the glories of Edom (1Chr 1:44). Esau had said, what profit shall this birthright do to me? (Gen 25:32), and he sold it for a morsel; his sons gained the earthly dignity he had coveted, and held it but for a breath. Bozrah’s king is dust, and Bozrah itself a witness against the pride of Edom. But the LORD reigneth from Bozrah of another and a glorious sort, travelling in the greatness of His strength, mighty to save (Isa 63:1). The crowns of Esau perish; the crown of the true King abideth.

etymology: Hebrew husham, “haste” or “hasting,” the name of the third king of Edom, of the land of Temani, who reigned after Jobab.
biblical_def: Husham of the land of Temani reigned in Edom after the death of Jobab (Gen 36:34). He is the third in the line of kings who reigned in the land of Esau before any king reigned over the children of Israel (Gen 36:31). The land of Temani takes its name from Teman, a grandson of Esau and a duke of Edom (Gen 36:11,15), and Teman became a byword for the wisdom of Edom, that wisdom which the prophet declares the LORD will utterly destroy: Is wisdom no more in Teman? (Jer 49:7); Shall I not in that day, saith the LORD, even destroy the wise men out of Edom, and understanding out of the mount of Esau? (Oba 1:8). Husham, then, came of the land most renowned for Edom’s counsel and prudence, and yet his reign too is summed in the same two words as all the rest: he reigned, and he died (Gen 36:35). The wisdom of Teman could not preserve its king from the grave, nor Edom from the doom pronounced against the mount of Esau. Herein the Holy Ghost rebukes all carnal wisdom that boasteth itself against the LORD. The understanding of the prudent shall be hid, and the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God (1Cor 1:20). Husham of Temani reigned and perished; but the fear of the LORD, that is wisdom, and it abideth for ever.

etymology: Hebrew hadad, “mighty” or “fierce” (a name borne also by an Edomite idol), the name of the fourth king of Edom, the son of Bedad, of the city Avith.
biblical_def: Hadad the son of Bedad reigned in Edom after the death of Husham (Gen 36:35). He is the fourth king in the line of Esau, and of him alone among these kings is a deed of war recorded: he smote Midian in the field of Moab. The name of his city was Avith. This Hadad was a man of might in his generation, prevailing over Midian upon Moab’s plain, and yet his conquest is set in the same dry catalogue with all the others, for the Holy Ghost will not let the warrior boast: Hadad smote Midian, and Hadad died (Gen 36:36). The name Hadad was borne also by an idol of the Syrians and Edomites, a thing of nought; and so the very names of Esau’s kings carry the savour of the false worship that filled the land. Edom was lifted up in worldly pride and in might, and Edom shall be brought down. The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee, thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock (Oba 1:3). Hadad’s sword could subdue Midian, but it could not stay his own death, nor purchase his soul, nor stand against the LORD who weigheth the nations as the small dust of the balance. Here is the lesson of every conqueror of the earth: he prevaileth for an hour and then lieth down, and the kingdom passeth to another. Only the King who conquered death reigneth and dieth no more.

etymology: Hebrew samlah, “a garment” or “raiment,” the name of the fifth king of Edom, of the city Masrekah, who reigned after Hadad.
biblical_def: Samlah of Masrekah reigned in Edom after the death of Hadad the son of Bedad (Gen 36:36). He is the fifth king in the line of Esau that reigned before any king reigned over the children of Israel (Gen 36:31). His name signifies a garment, and his record, like a garment, is quickly folded away: he reigned, and he died, and Saul of Rehoboth rose up in his stead (Gen 36:37). The chronicle of the kings repeats his name and his city that the reader of after generations might know how the kingship of Edom passed from man to man, none of them founding an abiding house, none of them transmitting the crown to his own son, but each succeeded by a stranger out of another city (1Chr 1:47). Herein is a mark of the curse upon profane Edom, that her kingship had no rest nor settled root. The garment of earthly royalty was put on and laid aside again and again, while the kingdom promised to the seed of Jacob waited to be established for ever in David and in David’s greater Son. They all shall wax old as doth a garment; and as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed (Heb 1:12). The kings of Edom are folded up like raiment; but the LORD is the same, and His years shall not fail.

etymology: Hebrew sha’ul, “asked” or “asked of God,” the name of the sixth king of Edom, of Rehoboth by the river; not to be confounded with Saul the first king of Israel.
biblical_def: Saul of Rehoboth by the river reigned in Edom after the death of Samlah of Masrekah (Gen 36:37). He is the sixth king in the line of Esau that reigned before any king reigned over the children of Israel (Gen 36:31). His name in the Hebrew is the same that was borne long after by Saul the son of Kish, the first king of Israel; yet the reader must take heed not to confound the two, for this Saul was an Edomite of Rehoboth by the river, far removed in place and people from the Benjamite anointed by Samuel. The name sha’ul signifies “asked,” one sought or requested; and there is a solemn irony that the kings of Edom rose unasked of the LORD, while Israel in after days asked herself a king to her hurt (1Sam 8:5). Saul of Rehoboth reigned, and Saul died, and Baal-hanan rose up in his stead (Gen 36:38). The chronicle of the kings sets down his name with the rest (1Chr 1:48), that the reader might mark the steady tread of death through all the pomp of Edom. Esau was the profane brother (Heb 12:16); his kings reigned and died, asked or unasked. But the true King was given to Israel not at her asking but by the eternal counsel of God, and He reigneth and dieth no more.

etymology: Hebrew ba’al hanan, “Baal is gracious” or “the lord is gracious,” the name of the seventh king of Edom, the son of Achbor, who reigned after Saul.
biblical_def: Baal-hanan the son of Achbor reigned in Edom after the death of Saul of Rehoboth (Gen 36:38). He is the seventh king in the line of Esau that reigned before any king reigned over the children of Israel (Gen 36:31). His name is compounded of Baal, the great idol of the Canaanites and the nations round about, and hanan, “is gracious”: so the very name of this king of Edom ascribes grace to a false god, a thing of nought, and bears witness to the idolatry that filled the land of Esau. There is no grace in Baal, who is no god, but the Edomites named their children after him as men trusting in lies. Baal-hanan reigned, and Baal-hanan died, and Hadar rose up in his stead (Gen 36:39); the chronicle of the kings sets his name with the rest (1Chr 1:49). How vain to call upon Baal as gracious, when grace is the LORD’s alone, who is gracious and full of compassion (Psa 145:8), and who hath said, I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious (Exo 33:19). Edom looked to Baal and perished; the elect of God look to the LORD and are saved. Esau was profane (Heb 12:16), and his land was given over to false worship; but the LORD is gracious indeed, and there is no other Saviour beside Him. Let no man ascribe to an idol the grace that belongs to the living God.

corruption_paragraphs: Baal-hanan the son of Achbor is a figure of the sacred register, the seventh king of Edom, whose name is compounded with Baal, the idol of the nations. No movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine him; the dictionary records him that the reader may know him for a real king whose very name testifies to the idolatry of Esau’s land.

Here the biblical corruption is named plainly in Scripture’s own vocabulary: idolatry and false worship. To call Baal “gracious” is to ascribe to a thing of nought the grace that is the LORD’s alone (Exo 33:19; Psa 145:8). Esau was profane (Heb 12:16), and his sons looked to Baal and perished. The principle to recover is that grace belongs to the living God only, and there is no Saviour beside Him; let no man render unto an idol the mercy that is the LORD’s.

etymology: Hebrew hadar, “honour” or “ornament” (written Hadad in 1Chr 1:50), the name of the last named king of Edom, of the city Pau.
biblical_def: Hadar reigned in Edom after the death of Baal-hanan the son of Achbor, and he is the last named of the kings of Edom in the generations of Esau (Gen 36:39). The name of his city was Pau; and his wife’s name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab. He is the only one of these kings whose death is not recorded in the chronicle, and the only one whose wife and her lineage are set down, as though the register pauses at the last to mark the end of the line. In the parallel place he is called Hadad (1Chr 1:50), a small variance of the letters that the diligent reader will not stumble at. His name signifies honour or ornament; yet the honour of Edom was a fading flower, for after these kings the rule passed to the dukes, and at the last to the desolation pronounced by the prophets. As for Edom, I will lay it desolate (Eze 35:15); and, They shall call it, The border of wickedness, and, The people against whom the LORD hath indignation for ever (Mal 1:4). Hadar’s honour was but for a season. The Holy Ghost closes the catalogue of Edom’s kings with a marriage and a city, then turns the page to the dukes and to the doom; but Israel’s King is crowned with honour that fadeth not, and His name endureth for ever.

corruption_paragraphs: Hadar of Pau is a figure of the sacred register, the last named king of Edom, whose wife and her lineage alone are recorded among these kings. No movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine him; the dictionary records him that the reader may know him for a real king who closes the line, and that Hadar and Hadad are one name in the two registers.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the brevity of all worldly honour against the everlasting honour of God’s King. Hadar’s name means honour, yet Edom’s honour faded, and the LORD laid Esau’s heritage waste (Mal 1:3). Esau was profane (Heb 12:16). The catalogue of Edom’s kings ends with a marriage and a desolation; but Israel’s King is crowned with honour that fadeth not.

etymology: Hebrew timna’, “restraint” or “allotted portion,” the name of a duke of Edom reckoned among the dukes of Esau by their families and their places (Gen 36:40); distinct from Timna the concubine of Eliphaz.
biblical_def: Duke Timnah is named first in the roll of the dukes that came of Esau, according to their families, after their places, by their names (Gen 36:40). After the line of kings was ended, the rule of Edom is reckoned by dukes, that is, chieftains or heads of clans, each ruling over his own families and their dwelling places. The reader must take heed to distinguish this duke Timnah from Timna the concubine of Eliphaz, who was sister to Lotan and mother of Amalek (Gen 36:12,22); the same name is borne by more than one in the generations of Esau, as is common in the genealogies. The name timna’ may signify restraint, or an allotted portion; and there is a fitness in it, for the dukes of Edom held each his portion of that mountainous land, the possession the LORD had given to the children of Esau for Esau’s sake (Deu 2:5). Yet Edom held his portion in pride and not in fear of the LORD, and the prophets declare it shall be taken from him. Duke Timnah heads the list of these chieftains, the inheritors of a worldly dominion that the day of the LORD shall overthrow. Edom shall be a desolation (Jer 49:17); but the meek shall inherit the earth, and the portion of the saints is the LORD Himself, an inheritance incorruptible that fadeth not away.

etymology: Hebrew ’iram, “belonging to a city” or “watchful,” the name of the last named of the dukes of Edom in the generations of Esau (Gen 36:43).
biblical_def: Duke Iram is the last named of the dukes of Edom, set down at the close of the roll of Esau’s chieftains: Duke Magdiel, duke Iram: these be the dukes of Edom, according to their habitations in the land of their possession: he is Esau the father of the Edomites (Gen 36:43). With this name the long chapter of Esau’s generations is sealed, and the inspired writer adds the solemn summary, he is Esau the father of the Edomites, that no reader might forget the root from whence this nation sprang. Edom is Esau (Gen 36:1,8), the profane brother who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright and found no place of repentance (Heb 12:16–17); and all these dukes and kings, for all their crowns and habitations, are but the seed of him that despised the promise. The chapter ends, and the Spirit of God turns from the genealogy of the rejected to the history of the chosen, from Esau to Jacob, from Edom to Israel. Have not I loved Jacob? saith the LORD: yet I loved Jacob, and I hated Esau (Mal 1:2–3); as it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated (Rom 9:13). Duke Iram closes the line of them whom God passed by; and the closing word, he is Esau, is a warning to every man not to be a profane person, lest he sell an eternal birthright for the pottage of a day.

corruption_paragraphs: Duke Iram is a figure of the sacred register, the last named of the dukes of Edom, after whom the inspired writer sets the seal, he is Esau the father of the Edomites. No movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine him; the dictionary records him that the reader may know him for the close of Esau’s generations, and the turning-point from the rejected line to the chosen.

Here the biblical truth is named plainly in Scripture’s own vocabulary: Esau was a profane person, who sold his birthright for one morsel of meat (Heb 12:16). The closing word, he is Esau, gathers all these kings and dukes under the head of the profane brother whom God passed by: Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated (Rom 9:13; Mal 1:2–3). The principle to recover is the sovereign distinguishing love of God in election, and the warning that no man barter an eternal birthright for the pottage of a day.
